newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to tender for new digital telephone system.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to tender for new digital telephone system.

text.p: Turkey is working on a plan to tender soon for its second digital telecommunication system to meet a growing demand for mobile telephones, Transport Minister Omer Barutcu said on Wednesday.
"We will soon announce a tender to give two licenses under the DCS-1800 system. The technical work for the tender is under way," Barutcu told Reuters.
Turkey has been using the Global System for Mobiles (GSM) since early 1995 under two licenses given to two companies -- Turkcell and Telsim.
Both companies have local and foreign partners, with Turkcell having the Swedish company Ericsson and Telsim the U.S. firm Motorola as major partners.
"The two new companies will compete in a manner similar to how Turkcell and Telsim have been competing in the local market," Barutcu said.
Telecommunication officials said they expected the interest for the tender to be high, but did not say how much the project would be worth.
They said the DCS-1800 system was a separate digital telephone network which has a 1,800 MegaHertz (MHz) frequency capacity, compared to 900 Mhz of the GSM standard.
"The GSM system has 700,000 subscribers now and can have up to 1.5 million in total, a number which will cause congestion in frequency distribution," said one transport ministry official.
He said there could be as many as 10 million subscribers with the new DCS-1800 system.
Officials said some French and British companies as well as big Turkish companies had shown interest in the tender.

Turkey's state-run telecommunications company Turk Telekom, slated for privatisation in 1994 and the centre-piece for the government's ambitious privatisation programme, signed revenue-sharing contracts with Turkcell and Telsim in 1993 for establishing digital switching systems and GSM networks.

Barutcu said the government would soon discuss the transferring this year of Turk Telekom's two GSM licences for about $500 million each to Turkcell and Telsim under 25-year contracts as part of its 1997 privatisation programme.

The constitutional court, Turkey's top legal body, paved the way for Turk Telekom's privatisation in January by annulling a legislative challenge by opposition MPs, who said the law governing the sell-off was against the constitution.
